[~accountid:61f116071c42100069544016] [~accountid:62a3287576c0360069f59b72] , has anything changed in the meantime?

Additionally, there is no legal requirement for mandatory liability insurance for scooters that do not require registration, so we are not obligated to have one.

Therefore, I would first wait for [~accountid:61f116071c42100069544016] ' response. If there is no insurance in place, I would inform the police that we do not have one and are not legally required to, as our e-scooters do not require registration.

However, please note that we might receive a claim for damages from the owner of the damaged car. According to the Law of Obligations, if we cannot prove that someone else was using the e-scooter without our permission, we, as the owner, are liable for the damages.

{noformat}%sql

The user is reporting a double-charge because of incremental authorization.
Incremental authorization in card payments refers to the process of requesting an additional authorization on a customer’s card when the original authorized amount is insufficient to cover the final transaction cost. This typically happens in scenarios where the final amount of the transaction is not known upfront or may change.

I have checked the case and everything looks good on Bolt’s end. The pre-authorization has been released to the customer. 
You can ask the customer to reach out to their bank in order to confirm the authorized funds have been released. Their bank can locate the funds with the authorization date and amount.

Hello Steve,

We discussed this with my manager. Yes, the current process in Workday should be changed and unpaid leave should not generate annual leave accrual for the following reasons:

1) it based on Estonian payroll legislation 

2) info at Bolt Confluence says:

+“Unpaid Leave+ - this leave should be agreed with your manager beforehand.
Some things to keep in mind if you take this leave for more than 2 weeks:

* _your annual leave accrual will be paused”_[https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/BILP/pages/1596654634/Estonia#Study-Leave-%F0%9F%93%9A|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/BILP/pages/1596654634/Estonia#Study-Leave-%F0%9F%93%9A|smart-link] 



Would it be possible for your team to implement a solution that stops annual leave accrual in Estonia for unpaid leave periods longer than two weeks?

We understand that pro-rating accrual based on the exact number of unpaid leave days would be complex. Instead, a simpler approach might be to introduce a restriction during the absence request process in Workday.

Last Friday 07.02.2025 we tested together with Arina Vorozhtsova the accruals of annual leave during unpaid leave periods for Estonia. There are 2 types of unpaid leaves:

* EST Unpaid leave: accrual *would not be paused* (this type should be used for periods 1-14 calendar days).
* GBL Unpaid leave (long-term): accrual *would be paused automatically* (this type should be used for periods 14+ calendar days).

For the experiment I am myself trying to request the unpaid leave in Workday for period 01.03 - 23.03.2025:

Time and Absence - Request Absence - Type of Absence. Here the employee has to choose the type of absence:

!Screenshot 2025-02-10 at 10.22.54.png|width=445,height=605,alt="Screenshot 2025-02-10 at 10.22.54.png"!

My unpaid leave lasts 23 days (it is 14+ days, so should be classified as GBL Unpaid leave (long-term) and accrual should stop). But if I go to Long Term Leaves, I can choose *only* Maternity Leave (please see the printscreen below):

!Screenshot 2025-02-10 at 10.26.21.png|width=443,height=299,alt="Screenshot 2025-02-10 at 10.26.21.png"!

So I have no other option but I have to go to Short Term Leaves and to choose EST Unpaid leave:

!Screenshot 2025-02-10 at 10.28.58.png|width=430,height=637,alt="Screenshot 2025-02-10 at 10.28.58.png"!

But this is wrong, as my leave is 14+ days and the only option “EST Unpaid leave” does not stop the accrual. I also have another example: employee Chiara Lionel Salim could easily take “EST Unpaid Leave” for 3 month 27.01 - 02.05.2025. I am certain that such possibilities should be restricted in the future.

h4. The solution could be as follows:

* If an employee requests unpaid leave for *1 to 14 days*, they would only be able to select *“EST Unpaid Leave”* under _Short-Term Leaves_, and accrual *would not be paused*.
* If an employee requests unpaid leave for *15 or more days*, they would not be able to select an option under _Short-Term Leaves anymore_ (a restriction should be applied based on the period). Instead, they would only be able to select *“GBL Unpaid Leave (Long-term)”* under _Long-Term Leaves_, and accrual would be *paused automatically* for the duration of the unpaid leave.

Would this solution be feasible? Or do you have any other suggestions? 

Looking forward to your thoughts.

Best regards,

Evgenia

The error message *"82 : Negative CAM, dCVV, iCVV, CVV, or CAVV results"* is a *credit card transaction decline code* related to *card verification failure*.

h3. Explanation:

* *CAM (Card Authentication Method)*, *dCVV (Dynamic CVV)*, *iCVV (Integrated Circuit Card CVV)*, *CVV (Card Verification Value)*, and *CAVV (Cardholder Authentication Verification Value)* are security features used to verify the authenticity of a card.
* A *negative result* means that the verification check *failed*, so the transaction is declined for security reasons.



Please ask the customer to do the following: 

* *Double-check the card details* (CVV, expiration date, and card number).
* *Try a different card* or payment method.
* *Contact the card issuer* (bank) to see if there’s a block on the transaction.
* *For online transactions, ensure 3D Secure authentication is completed properly*.


Cheers,
Marten

Based on your ticket, I see a few points to address:

* Integration doesn’t have the option to extract specific expense reports from the system. If any were omitted from the ZIP file you received, it means that the integration encountered an issue processing the attachments, and these expenses must be processed manually.
* The ZIP folder for expenses always uses the accounting date to extract documents from Workday - this has not changed since the integration was first implemented.
* For invoices, it is possible to retrieve data using two date parameters: accounting date and invoice creation date in the system.

After the integration event is completed, a file named "Message Logs.html" will also be available in the "output files" section. This file contains three tabs: ERRORS, WARNINGS and INFO. The ERRORS tab provides information about documents that encountered technical issues during integration and require manual processing.

More information you can find also on [workday-faq-finance|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C02NN7CANGJ/p1738859958464699] slack channel.

{quote}how come that we have PRICE CHANGED error on the first item that is being added to basket?{quote}

The price seen by the customer and provided as payload of /addBasketItem is different from what we see on the BE side, hence the error. As discussed in DM, perhaps we should add the item, but alert the user that the price changed, or rely on the checkout summary to do so.

As I understand, here we first create the basket, then add the basket item, then on failure we refresh the basket summary. But because we create the basket as part of the adding the first basket item, we don’t store the basket info just yet, and we fail to refresh the basket summary.

Ideas:

* create and store basket details, even if there is no items at all
* or do not request basket summary, if we don't have stored basket (and there is no reason to refetch empty basket).
So we need to put a check before adding basket summary request

To check:

* what side effects we might have in this case. Likely everything will be fine, but to avoid cases like Basket button that leads to empty basket.

h4. Root Cause

We were using a "User Verified" event passed to Firebase for Google Ads Signup calculations. This event, unfortunately, includes repeat verifications from returning users, leading to double-counting of signups. We have now corrected this and are passing a "First User Verified" event to Firebase, which accurately reflects new user signups without duplicates. Going forward, all CLS experiments should use this "First User Verified" event for signup tracking.

*Current context:*
Right now, when we create the live db, we assume that all the shards have the same schema, so we skip the duplicates: [code.|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/ec9f78f31353e22f0d9cee44a6703f29594407f3/tooling_scripts/gen/db/create-live-db-sql.js#L37]

*New Approach:* 

* If the schema is sharded, we will append the {{shard_name}} to the {{schema_name}} to be able to create the database, otherwise duplicates are not allowed (see more [here|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/ec9f78f31353e22f0d9cee44a6703f29594407f3/tooling_scripts/gen/db/create-live-db-sql.js#L37]). 
** Note: We can use the format {{shard_name_schema_name}} to avoid potential conflicts. 
* When exporting the schemas, we will generate N SQL files per schema, where N represents the number of shards. 
* The next step is to compare th[e local schemas with the live ones|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/03227f76799e4a8b975c8da7c2dd991cf3da45fc/tooling_scripts/db/diff/schema_diff.sh#L71]. 
** In this stage, we will have to match and compare the local schema with all live schemas (if they are sharded; otherwise, it will be just one live schema) and generate a single diff for all of them.

Notes: The tool is not suitable for comparing between shards. Additionally, it requires precomputing all combinations of diffs between shards.

Hey [~accountid:712020:1a3a17cb-2e37-4162-8d95-4d1059255d7e] ,

We have received this answer from their lawyers :

“Antes de avançarmos com comentários detalhados ao contrato, gostaríamos de obter alguns esclarecimentos essenciais:

# Em várias cláusulas do contrato (por exemplo, cláusula 3, nº 5 e cláusula 17), é mencionado que a Bolt estará em conformidade com o Contrato de Concessão entre a Movicovilhã e o Município de Covilhã, incluindo no que respeita a sanções e penalizações. Consideramos esta exigência desproporcional, dado que a Bolt não teve qualquer envolvimento na celebração desse Contrato de Concessão e está, na prática, a ser utilizada para cumprir obrigações contratuais assumidas pela Movicovilhã perante o Município.

Dado o impacto que este ponto pode ter, solicitamos que indiquem especificamente quais as cláusulas do Caderno de Encargos da concessão que fundamentam estas obrigações.

*R:* Em primeiro lugar, não conseguimos identificar o n.º 5 da Cláusula 3.ª a que se referem. Na última versão do Contrato partilhada, a Cláusula 3.ª tem apenas quatro número.

 

Seja como for, entendemos que as obrigações em causa não são desproporcionais, A Cláusula 17.ª (Back-to-back) é comum em contratos deste tipo, celebrados ao abrigo de contratos de concessão, e justifica-se precisamente em virtude dessa circunstância. Como o propósito do contrato a celebrar entre a Movicovilhã e a Bolt é regular os termos em que esta cumprirá determinadas obrigações decorrentes do Contrato de Concessão para a Movicovilhã, é essencial garantir um princípio de absoluta transparência entre ambos os instrumentos contratuais.

 

Dito isto, a Cláusula 17.ª é clara ao limitar o âmbito de relevância do princípio back-to-back às “_obrigações assumidas ao abrigo do presente contrato_”, o que significa que a Bolt assume as obrigações previstas no contrato a celebrar com a Movicovilhã, embora deva cumpri-las em conformidade com o disposto no Contrato de Concessão. No fundo, o que se pretende é que as Partes tenham conhecimento absoluto da sua posição relativa no contrato e consciência do seu enquadramento jurídico, de forma que o contrato seja executado de acordo com os interesses das Partes.

 

No que respeita, por sua vez, à menção a sanções e penalizações, a Movicovilhã recorda que, nos termos da Cláusula 12.ª do contrato a celebrar com a Bolt, é aplicável, com as devidas adaptações, o regime sancionatório previsto no Contrato de Concessão. Ou seja, em vez de criar um regime sancionatório de raiz, propõem a adaptação, ao presente contrato, das normas que regulam a aplicação de sanções no âmbito do Contrato de Concessão. Isto não significa que a Bolt esteja exposta a um maior risco de aplicação de sanções, mas apenas que às situações de eventual incumprimento apuradas durante a execução do contrato será aplicado – reitera-se, com as devidas adaptações – o regime sancionatório do Contrato de Concessão.

 

A Movicovilhã sublinha, à luz de todo o exposto supra, que o teor das cláusulas em questão é razoável, não impondo às Partes – em particular, à Bolt – obrigações desmesuradas ou desproporcionais, e justifica-se em razão da subordinação do contrato a celebrar entre a Movicovihã e a Bolt ao Contrato de Concessão em vigor.

# A cláusula 6 do contrato prevê que a Bolt cumpra os Regulamentos Municipais de Mobilidade, que permitem a utilização por menores de idade (16 e 17 anos) desde que possuam uma declaração de responsabilidade assinada pelos pais ou representantes legais.

Esta disposição é incompatível com os nossos Termos e Condições, pelo que não pode ser aceite nos termos atuais. Gostaríamos de saber se a Movicovilhã está disposta a abdicar desta exigência ou, em alternativa, aceitar que a Bolt cumpra os Regulamentos Municipais apenas na medida em que sejam compatíveis com os nossos T&C.

*R*: A Movicovilhã tem consciência das dificuldades subjacentes à harmonização dos T&C da Bolt com o disposto no Regulamento de Utilização de Veículos do Serviço Público de Mobilidade Suave Partilhada, e entende que a eliminação desse obstáculo terá, necessariamente, de envolver o Município.

 

Por esse motivo, embora não se oponha, por princípio, à introdução de uma ressalva nos termos propostos na V/ comunicação, de acordo com a qua a vinculação da Bolt ao regulamento se cinge às disposições que não contrariem o disposto nos T&C, essa medida é, por si, insuficiente.

 

Assim, a Movicovilhã propõe que se coloque à consideração do Município que aos menores de 16 e 17 anos apenas seja permitida a utilização de bicicletas no âmbito do sistema público de mobilidade suave partilhada.”

Hello! The data is provided here: [https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1JJ60prFNKO8qUGCnQFv-KKMrV0LM5aXlv7iWHhAfZZo/edit?gid=1642850274#gid=1642850274|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1JJ60prFNKO8qUGCnQFv-KKMrV0LM5aXlv7iWHhAfZZo/edit?gid=1642850274#gid=1642850274]

the query used: 

{noformat}with rides_data as (
	select 
		'ride' as order_type,
		co.id, 
		co.created_date,
		co.country,
		bc.country_code,
		bc.name,
		co.user_id,
		cot.price,
		cot.price_currency as currency
	from company_order co
	left join company_order_try cot on cot.order_id = co.id and cot.city_id = co.city_id and cot.retry_to_try is null
	left join etl_business_business_company bc on bc.id = cast(regexp_extract(payment_method_id, '^\d+') as int)
	where regexp_like(payment_method_id, '^\d+') 
	and payment_method_type = 'business'
	and date(co.created_date) between  date '2024-01-01'  and date '2025-01-01'
	and is_bolt_company
	and co.state = 'finished'
	--and co.user_id = 157724762
),
rentals_data as (
	select 
		'rental' as order_type,
		roo.id,
		roo.created_date,
		roo.country,
		bc.country_code,
		bc.name,
		roo.user_id,
		roo.price,
		roo.currency 
	from ng_rental.rental_order_order roo
	left join etl_business_business_company bc on bc.id = cast(regexp_extract(payment_method_id, '^\d+') as int)
	where regexp_like(payment_method_id, '^\d+') 
	and payment_method_type  = 'business'
	and date(roo.created_date) between  date '2024-01-01'  and date '2025-01-01'
	and bc.is_bolt_company 
	and roo.state = 'finished'
	--and roo.user_id = 157724762
), 
all_data as ( 
	select * from rides_data
	union
	select * from rentals_data
), 
all_data_to_eur as (
	select 
	ad.order_type,
	ad.id,
	ad.created_date,
	ad.country,
	ad.country_code,
	ad.name,
	ad.user_id,
	ad.price as price_lcc,
	ad.currency,
	ad.price/r.rate as price_eur
	from all_data as ad
	left join ng_public.vw_currency_exchange_rates as r on ad.currency = r.currency 
														and date(ad.created_date) = date(r.valid_on)
	order by created_date
)
select 
	country,
--	country_code,
--	name,
	count(distinct user_id) as users_count,
	round(sum(price_eur),1) as credit_used_eur
from all_data_to_eur
where name like 'Bolt Technology%'
group by 1;{noformat}

Follow up questions with their answers are as follows:

# *Can minors act as independent couriers and/or fleet couriers? What are the requirements for both options?*

*Independent couriers* have to set up a trade license. According to the Trade Licensing Act, one of the general conditions for those interested is that they must be above 18 years old. Since 2014, however, the Civil Code has also given minors the opportunity to run a business. They currently have the following three options. *However, all of them require a decision or permission from the court, making this option rather unrealistic*. If the number of hours worked is less than 300 hours per year, it is not necessary to set up a trade license but to conclude an agreement to perform a job (see below).

# *The minor, with the consent of his/her legal representative*, appoints a responsible representative who must meet the general and special conditions for operating a trade according to the Trade Licensing Act. *This appointment must subsequently be approved by the court. Subsequently, the legal representative shall register the trade or apply for a licence on behalf of the minor with the trade licensing office.* In this case, the responsibility for the work carried out lies with the minor, but the responsible representative will be responsible for the proper operation of the trade and for compliance with the trade law.
# A minor may engage in an independent business on the basis of *the court's approval of the legal representative's consent to the independent operation of a business establishment or other similar gainful activity*. The minor must present his or her business plan to the court, demonstrating his or her maturity or, for example, that he or she can combine the business with health or schooling. In particular, the court will weigh the mental maturity of the minor against the difficulty and time-consuming nature of the activity for which he or she intends to obtain approval. There is no lower age limit for this application.
# A minor may also engage in business independently on the basis of *the court's recognition of his or her legal capacity.* If the court grants their application, they will not need a responsible representative and can make all business decisions on their own. If the court grants the minor legal capacity, their legal capacity will not be limited to business. However, it is necessary for him to fulfil more conditions than in the case of the court's authorisation to run a business or other similar gainful activity on his own. First of all, the *minor must be at least 16 years old and must prove that he is capable of supporting himself and providing for his own affairs.* He or she also needs the *consent of the legal guardian* in order for the court to grant permission.  

*Fleet couriers* must have an employment relationship with the fleet, i.e. agreement to perform a job (Dohoda o provedení práce - *DPP*) or agreement to work (Dohoda o pracovní činnosti - *DPČ*). Agreement to perform a job (DPP) is for occasional work of up to 300 hours per year for a single employer. The maximum working time for an agreement to work (DPČ) is set at 20 hours per week, for DPP it is maximum 300hours/year. These agreements can already be concluded by the minor independently, i.e. without the consent of the legal guardian. For both agreements, the rules of employment of minors that we have already emailed before apply, i.e. *it is forbidden to employ minors under the age of 15 or minors who have not completed compulsory schooling *(this is regulated, in addition to the Labour Code, by the Civil Code and the Employment Act).Other restrictions regarding the employment of minors according to the Labour Code include:

* The maximum working time shall be 40 hours per week and shall not exceed 8 hours in any one day. There must be a break of at least 12 hours between shifts. Minors must be given a break after four and a half hours of work
* Minors cannot work overtime.
* Minors cannot work in the night.
* There are also types of work that minors cannot do because they would be at increased risk of injury or endangering others. Examples include work involving the handling of loads, the manufacture and processing of explosives, work performed at an imposed pace, work performed in confined spaces or tanks, slaughtering animals in slaughterhouses, etc.
* Regarding the salary, the only restriction of salaries of minors is the minimum wage set by the government.

# *What documents are required (e.g., parental consent, specific work permits) during the sign-up/onboarding process?*

All requirements are listed in the first answer.

# *Other requirements: any further considerations or restrictions we should be aware of? (e.g. limitations on delivery of certain (age-restricted) items?*

Minor couriers cannot deliver alcohol or tobacco products. According to the Ordinance on Prohibited Work and Workplaces, minors under 18 cannot perform physically demanding work, at which the hygienic energy intake limits for girls or boys are exceeded. Girls should also not handle weights over 15 kg and boys over 20 kg.

I went through the documentation and I think that we can stick to our claim (given that the vehicle had keys, not in-app locking):

# It was an ongoing ride and you have the duty of care to make sure that you have your ignition keys with you. As a rule, insurance funds refuse the claims where you have left the keys inside the vehicle. Even if we have had a _kasko_-insurance this would have not been paid out because the user left the keys inside and this was the root cause of the incident.
# We have a contractual relationship with the client. The damage was caused while the vehicle was under their control. They can reclaim the damages from the perpetrator but we should not be a hostage to this situation.

Essentially, I see no reason why we couldn’t claim this. We can make some concessions and agree on a schedule, for example. But this situation would not have been if the user would have been diligent and taken the keys.

Advice from PP external counsel:

*In accordance with the Civil Code section § 656 we are obliged to store the unclaimed parcels (meaning that the receiver wasn't able to collect it and the sender was also unavailable) for at least 6 months. Are we required to obtain a license for that kind of a situation?*

According to the current law, *there is no such special obligation*, however, bear in mind that any warehouse *must meet the basic conditions including hygienic rules or rules on safety and protection at work* (very similar to warehouses with e-scooters). Please, find [here|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1f4TWftPId6SgsM_mRv53dJM8oJ_a58P8/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=117683158400867349959&rtpof=true&sd=true] the list of the key conditions we prepared for rentals in August 2024.

Furthermore, the six-month period mentioned in §656 (which is just reference to §765-§773 - Cargo transportation contracts), does really state the six-month period, however, as mentioned in the analysis, *application of these provisions depends on the business model* and whether the package processed by Bolt is considered to be a parcel or a package (in other words, *whether an object that is being sent meets the conditions of a parcel according to §5 of the Act on Postal Services*).

In case the Civic code is applied, it is important to point out the §773 par. 2, which says: *_Transport terms may specify periods shorter than 6 months_* _for the collection (removal) of certain shipments,_ *_especially items of a dangerous nature or items that spoil quickly_*_._ This means the period *can be reduced under some conditions* and is not strictly set to 6 months.

In case the Act on Postal Services is applied, the time obligations related to storing unclaimed parcels are defined by *§34 par. 6 of the Act on Postal Services, which says the maximum is six months*, however, in case of parcels *without dispatch receipts, the maximum period is just three months.* The period *can also be longer than six months,* if a complaint is made, a claim for damages is made or a dispute is resolved alternatively (following Act on Alternative resolution of consumer disputes), in which case the storage period is extended until the expiry of the period in which all legal means to achieve redress can be used. Note that subsequent *removal of unclaimed parcels according to the Act on Parcel Services is strictly regulated (§34)*, especially due to the basic human right of secrecy of correspondence entrenched in Article 22 of the Slovak constitution.

As mentioned in our analysis, *we recommend a proper legal counselling in this area* as the rules and conditions are heavily dependent on the business model and conditions under which Bolt provides delivery services.

Hey! 



There is no special insurance in place for the Lithuanian market.

All vehicles require an MTPL policy, and in most countries, the passengers are also covered (even if no other vehicle or third party was involved in the accident). 

Furthermore, when talking about taxi/ridehailing services, many licensing authorities require a special taxi/private hire licence from the driver. With those licences, often further insurance coverage is required from the driver (providing a higher level of protection to the passengers). 

In most markets where such requirements apply, Bolt as the ridehailing operator is often required to keep copies of such licences/policies, i.e. these are often requested by Bolt from the driver during the onboarding process. 

If what I have described above, is also applicable to LT, then this could be used as one of the examples of how Bolt secures that the passengers will be compensated when an accident occurs. 

However, if that is not the case for LT, I’m afraid the only protection we currently have is the MTPL. If the client requires any further protection, we can explore obtaining a business liability coverage for Bolt. 



Best

Karmel

*Prompt:* What should an EU-based carsharing company bear in mind from legal and privacy standpoints when establishing a decentralised database containing blacklisted carsharing users from different carsharing companies, so that the information could be used by all of them in order to keep bad users away and prevent them to rent cars?

*Output:* An EU-based carsharing company looking to establish a decentralized blacklist database shared among multiple companies must carefully navigate *data protection, competition, and consumer protection laws*. Key legal and privacy considerations include:

h3. *1. GDPR Compliance*

Since the blacklist will contain personal data (e.g., names, license numbers, past misconduct), compliance with the *General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)* is crucial:

* *Legal Basis (Art. 6 GDPR)*:
** *Legitimate interest (Art. 6(1)(f))* may be used, but a *balancing test* must show that preventing fraud outweighs users’ rights.
** *Contractual necessity (Art. 6(1)(b))* could apply if preventing fraud is an explicit condition in the rental agreement.
** *Consent (Art. 6(1)(a))* is difficult, as it must be freely given and revocable.
* *Data Minimization & Accuracy (Art. 5 GDPR)*: Only relevant and accurate data should be stored, with clear criteria for blacklisting.
* *Data Subject Rights (Arts. 15-22 GDPR)*: Users must have access, rectification, and appeal rights.
* *Storage Limitation (Art. 5 GDPR)*: A clear retention policy is needed to avoid indefinite blacklisting.
* *Cross-Border Data Sharing (Art. 46 GDPR)*: If the system involves non-EU entities, data transfer safeguards must be in place.

h3. *2. Competition Law Risks (Art. 101 TFEU)*

A shared blacklist among competitors might be seen as an *anti-competitive agreement*:

* If it *limits consumer access across providers*, regulators may view it as a *cartel-like restriction*.
* To mitigate risk, companies should ensure that *only serious infractions* (e.g., fraud, car theft, repeated unpaid fines) justify blacklisting.
* The database should be *administered independently*, with clear and *non-discriminatory access criteria*.

h3. *3. Consumer Protection Considerations*

* *Transparency*: Users must be informed in clear *Terms & Conditions* that misconduct may result in blacklisting.
* *Appeal Mechanism*: Users should be able to challenge incorrect blacklisting decisions before an independent body.
* *Non-discriminatory Application*: Blacklisting should be based on objective and proportionate criteria.

h3. *4. Decentralized vs. Centralized Architecture Risks*

* *A decentralized database (e.g., blockchain-based)* raises concerns about *data accuracy, rectification, and deletion (Art. 17 GDPR – Right to Erasure)*.
* If *no single entity "controls" the data*, identifying a *Data Controller* is complex, making compliance harder.
* A *governance structure* should define *who updates, deletes, and verifies records* to ensure compliance.

h3. *5. Data Security & Liability*

* *Cybersecurity measures (Art. 32 GDPR)*: Strong encryption and access controls must be in place.

*Prompt:* What should an EU-based carsharing company bear in mind, mainly from legal, privacy and payment regulation perspectives, when setting up a security deposit for users renting out cars whose amount may be based on the user's risk profile.

*Output:* When setting up a security deposit system based on users' risk profiles, an EU-based carsharing company should consider the following key legal, privacy, and payment regulation aspects:

h3. *1. Legal Considerations*

* *Unfair Contract Terms (UCTD Directive 93/13/EEC)*: Ensure the deposit terms are fair, proportionate, and transparent. Unreasonably high deposits could be deemed unfair and unenforceable.
* *Consumer Protection (Digital Services Act & Consumer Rights Directive 2011/83/EU)*: Clear disclosure of deposit amounts, calculation methods, and refund policies is required.
* *Anti-Discrimination (EU Charter & National Laws)*: Ensure risk profiling does not indirectly discriminate based on protected characteristics such as nationality or socio-economic status.

h3. *2. Privacy (GDPR Compliance)*

* *Legal Basis for Risk Profiling*:
** _Legitimate Interest_: Justifiable if necessary for fraud prevention, but a Legitimate Interest Assessment (LIA) is required.
** _Consent_: Required if profiling involves sensitive personal data.
* *Transparency & Data Minimization*:
** Inform users about profiling logic, deposit calculation criteria, and their rights (Articles 13 & 14 GDPR).
** Avoid excessive data collection and ensure deposits are proportionate to actual risk.
* *Automated Decision-Making (Article 22 GDPR)*: If the deposit is determined solely by an algorithm, users must be given the right to contest decisions and request human review.

h3. *3. Payment & Financial Regulations*

* *PSD2 (Directive (EU) 2015/2366) Compliance*:
** If deposits are pre-authorized on payment cards, ensure Strong Customer Authentication (SCA) is applied.
** Clearly state authorization holds and settlement rules to avoid disputes.
* *E-Money & Financial Licensing Risks*:
** If the deposit is _held_ (not just pre-authorized) and later refunded, it might be considered e-money under EU law, requiring a payment institution license.
* *Chargeback & Refund Policies*:
** Define clear timelines for deposit release to prevent payment disputes under PSD2 chargeback rules.
* *AML Compliance*: If handling large deposits, ensure adherence to Anti-Money Laundering (AML) regulations to mitigate risks of fraud.

Noticed that the  optimisation algorithm (pick the max discount which is above the given U/C threshold) doesn’t yield optimal results. Updated the algorithm to the logic below

- Compute the Convex Hull of discounts at user level (i.e remove the discounts which should never appear in the optimal solution at any budget. For eg: if 10% discount has an uplift 5 and cost 5 while 20% discount has uplift 10 and cost 8. 10% would never be part of optimal solution)
- Find the most optimal discount for each discount/user. Mark the U/C as priority
- Compute incremental U/C between consecutive discounts on the Convex Hull, Mark these values as priority for other discounts (this helps address if we should bump the discount to higher value if a session already got a discount)
- Apply threshold and choose all the options which are above that threshold. Changing threshold => changing budgets and these thresholds can be used as proxy for budgets in prod implementation

The performance improvement is visible after updating the algorithm. Backtesting plots for the new optimisation algorithm and old ones are document [in this sheet|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1aywxQZ8FmvH1DEUnjbaHJi7_d8jWAyxl3q0n6tWsV2s/edit?usp=sharing]

Some insights from backtesting below. Compared U/C vs budget curves for different models against LPCT (Performance on Train and test Data attached)

* Models are able to show improvement in the low budgets but unable to beat LPCT at budgets > 7% (test data performance)
* Performance can be affected by both models and optimisation
** *Optimisation:* I also realised that the optimisation logic I used earlier is not guaranteeing optimal allocation based on model predictions. I have updated this using ideas from [this|https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.11979] paper and the performance improved across models after this
** *Models:* I have some intuitions on where the models are not doing well (I think they are discriminating users/sessions for a given discount well but unable to quantify the sensitivity well i.e conversion as a function of discount for a given user). I will do some quick iterations this week to see if this can be improved
* Disclaimers (data related):
** This is just 1 week of DEX data which I validated on (1 week to train and 1 week to test)
** There are some biases in the data used. It is generated using data from DEX run of regular campaigns so at session level, it's not fully randomised (for eg: more sessions in the data for higher discounts and distribution of users could be slightly different based as inactive users having higher sessions)
** We also need to collect DEX data with session level randomisation to train and validate models ( I will share more on this)

** *acceptance_rate and driver_score* – minimum values of Acceptance rate and Driver Score
** *ppr* – point per ride
** *ppr_peak_hours* – points per ride in peak hours
** *loyalty_targets* – minimum points driver has to get for the tier
** *peak_hours* – peak hours by weekday in UTC timezone

* If the screenshot shows that a driver does have a Reward level, inform the FO

Chat GPT’s take on P2B:

*Prompt:* What should an EU-based carsharing company bear in mind and which changes should it implement in view of the so-called P2B EU Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2019/1150)? 

*Output:* The *P2B (Platform-to-Business) Regulation (EU) 2019/1150* applies to online intermediation services and online search engines that facilitate transactions between business users and consumers. If an *EU-based carsharing company* operates a *platform where independent businesses list and offer carsharing services*, it falls within the scope of this regulation. Below are the *key aspects to bear in mind* and the *changes to implement* to ensure compliance:

----

h3. *1. Ensure Transparency in Terms & Conditions*

* Clearly *define* and *communicate* the ranking, pricing, and access criteria for business users (e.g., fleet operators or private car owners listing vehicles).
* Provide *at least 15 days' notice* before modifying terms & conditions and ensure a simple process for business users to terminate the contract if they disagree.
* Specify the *reasons for suspension or termination* of business users from the platform.

h3. *2. Improve Ranking and Search Transparency*

* Clearly disclose *ranking parameters* affecting how listings appear (e.g., price, ratings, vehicle availability).
* If payments, commissions, or promotions influence ranking, this must be explicitly stated.

h3. *3. Clarify Data Access & Usage*

* Disclose *what data* the platform collects and how it is used.
* Specify *who has access* to business users' data and whether it is shared with third parties.

h3. *4. Ensure Fair Treatment of Business Users*

* If the platform offers its *own carsharing services* or is affiliated with any fleet operators, it must disclose whether its own services are treated more favorably.
* Explain the difference in treatment between different business users, if applicable.

h3. *5. Provide an Internal Complaint-Handling System*

* Implement a *free and easily accessible* dispute resolution system.
* Address complaints *within a reasonable timeframe* and keep records of handling procedures.

h3. *6. Facilitate Mediation*

* Identify at least *two independent mediators* for dispute resolution.
* Bear a reasonable proportion of mediation costs.

h3. *7. Compliance Enforcement & Penalties*

* Non-compliance can lead to *investigations by national authorities* and potential sanctions.
* Business users may *challenge unfair practices* in court.

----

h3. *Next Steps for Implementation*

✔ *Review and update platform terms & conditions* to align with transparency requirements.
✔ *Modify ranking algorithms* and ensure disclosures are easily accessible.
✔ *Enhance internal complaint-handling* processes and designate mediators.
✔ *Update data policies* to clarify usage and access rules.
✔ *Conduct a legal and operational review* to avoid unfair treatment of business users.

Transportation services are provided by independent drivers or taxi companies. The carriage agreement is directly concluded between the transportation service provider and the passenger, even though Bolt facilitates its conclusion via the Bolt platform.

As a result, these independent drivers or taxi companies assume all legal responsibilities typically attributed to transportation service providers under applicable laws, including the Lithuanian Road Transport Code. This includes, but is not limited to:

* Compliance with consumer protection laws
* Responsibility for damages affecting a passenger’s health or life
* Liability for accidents or damages involving passengers or third parties
* Adherence to licensing and insurance requirements
* Maintenance of vehicle roadworthiness

Under Lithuanian law, motor third-party liability insurance (MTPL) is the only mandatory insurance for drivers. However, drivers providing transportation services are not covered by standard MTPL insurance; instead, they must obtain a higher-risk (and more expensive) MTPL policy specifically designed for ride-hailing and taxi drivers. Without this specialized MTPL coverage, drivers cannot obtain a Lithuanian Transport Safety Administration (LTSA) license and are not permitted to engage in transportation services.

h1. Root cause

* Envoy PodDisruptionBudget was configured for Envoy Pods with {{maxUnavailable: 5%}}
* Each Envoy StatefulSet contained 12 replicas
* With the 5% maxUnavailable setting, only one Pod could be unavailable at any time
* Issues occurred with Spot instances in multiple scenarios:
** Multiple Spot instances (2+) received AWS interruption notifications simultaneously
** Spot instance interruption coincided with Envoy rolling updates

h1. Impact

* When multiple Pods required recreation, subsequent Pods were forced to wait beyond the 2-minute Spot termination timeout
* Some Pods were forcefully terminated without executing their preStop hooks, leading to potential service disruption

h1. Resolution

* PDB Optimization
** Increased maxUnavailable from 5% to 25% (up to 3 Pods can be unavailable simultaneously)
** This change accommodates multiple concurrent Spot instance interruptions
* PreStop Hook Enhancement
** Implemented enhanced connection draining logic with active connection monitoring
** Added smart connection tracking with optimized timeout settings
** Introduced a three-phase graceful shutdown sequence:
**# Stop accepting new connections
**# Monitor existing connections with improved metrics
**# Terminate only when the connection count reaches zero.
** Results:
*** The average wait time reduced from 55 seconds to 16 seconds
*** More reliable Pod termination process
*** Better handling of connection draining.

      approx_distinct(CASE WHEN co.user_price_eur > 0 THEN co.order_id END,0.0041) count_cancels_with_fee,

amatia.lomax: > *Fallback Charge Threshold:* _Input parameter / safety parameter. In case model does not recommend any values, this threshold will be used._ There are two reasons for this value. First, in case the model fails (due to technical issues or model is not trained etc), the system will use this value. Secondly, the model uses historical data to determine thresholds for each hexagon. However, there can be areas in the city where there have been no swaps performed (or very little like 2 or 3) such as outskirt areas and hence the model does not generate any recommendations. In those cases, the fallback threshold is used. It is recommended to keep it the same as minimum swap threshold so that tasks do not open and close automatically if a scooter is moved during a ride.

Regarding whether this would fall under Article 22 UK GDPR or not (I also mentioned this in one of the ODPO recommendations), I believe it would *not*:

* As I understand from the current documentation, we would not be increasing the commission, only decreasing it based on these certain metrics
* It would also not affect our logic when matching drivers to riders, i.e. the driver would still be offered the trip as they are right now, only with a decreased commission rate (if applicable)

** With this feature, we would not increase the commission that they’ve already been notified about. The commission could only be decreased
* Taking all of the above into account, with this feature, driver earnings for specific trips may only *increase*, but not *decrease* below what they’d usually earn - this is why I believe the outcome of this processing would not have significant effect on them

Highlighting separately here as well, I believe it’s extremely important to explain the feature and the logic high-level to the drivers, as with the ICO inquiry, we’ve received quite a lot of questions about the transparency regarding e.g. work allocation from ICO (e.g. there was a question on whether we provide any information to drivers in case a trip is not assigned to them due to their custom pricing being higher than the average in their area). For contractual purposes I’d differentiate only two roles: (i) a person accessing Card Management Application [currently “Account owner” under the T&Cs], and (ii) a person accessing Card User Application [currently “User” under the T&Cs. _Exmos. Senhores,_

_No que concerne ao Ofício remetido por V. Exas., vem a Bolt prestar os seguinte esclarecimentos:_

_Relativamente à informação requerida referentes aos fluxos financeiros, esclarece-se que, quando é realizado um reembolso total ao cliente, derivado de uma situação de incumprimento/culpa do motorista, é reembolsada ao cliente a totalidade da quantia por este paga, numa única transação._

_Neste ponto, o sistema operativo da Bolt não diferencia, no âmbito do valor total pago pelo cliente, qual o montante correspondente à comissão que a Bolt aufere e qual o montante remanescente referente à quantia recebida pelo motorista, após a dedução da referida comissão._

_O propósito deste procedimento é assegurar a rápida e imediata resposta ao cliente, aspeto que a Bolt considera ser da maior importância, particularmente numa situação em que a necessidade de reembolso provem de incumprimento/culpa do motorista. Considerando o foco e orientação da Bolt em prioritizar a solicitação do cliente, e considerando que a necessidade de reembolso foi originada por incumprimento/culpa do motorista devidamente comprovada, o valor total reembolsado é creditado da conta do motorista._

_Utilizando o exemplo providenciado por V. Elas., numa situação em que o cliente tenha pago 10€, este fluxo financeiro assegura que o cliente seja prontamente reembolsado da totalidade do montante pago, que corresponde a 10€ e não a 7,50€, que corresponde à quantia que o motorista iria receber._

_O montante remanescente de 2,5€ é posteriormente reembolsado ao motorista, num fluxo financeiro separado, sendo que os motoristas habitualmente reportam à Bolt, de forma direta, qualquer situação em que se verifique que algum montante se encontra em falta._

_Deste modo, na conclusão deste processo, o balanço final corresponde a 10€ para o cliente, e 0€ para a Bolt e para o motorista._

_Neste momento, a Bolt encontra-se a analisar potenciais melhorias a implementar neste procedimento, tendo em consideração as complexidades inerentes ao mesmo e a optimização dos fluxos financeiros de reembolso para todos os intervenientes._

_Atentamente,_

The flow of decision is the following:

**** If we see charge being unfair then we interrupt and say ‘NO CHARGE’

Meaning, in order to do abuse cancellation fees the drivers need to figure out not only the local logic but also bypass our fraud rules. Let’s see the volumes.

*So, broadly spoken currently we are around 87% sum / 81% count accurate with our apply_fee decisions based on the frequency of refunds monthly.* 

However, as mentioned, I’ll check if we can add some additional confidence to this metric as refunds in UK also happen for cases where rider complains but the driver has acted as expected to attend the order.

*Fraud decisions and refunds*

{noformat}SELECT 
CASE WHEN x.decision = 'apply_fee' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS apply_fee,
CASE WHEN x.amount_refunded > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS refunded,
approx_distinct(x.order_id,0.0041)AS count_orders,
round(sum(x.price_eur),0) AS sum_fees_eur,
round(sum(x.amount_refunded_eur),0) AS sum_refunded_fees_eur,
round(sum(x.amount_refunded_eur)*1.00/sum(x.price_eur),2) AS ratio_refunded
FROM 
(
  WITH checks AS 
  (
SELECT
uco.id,
--concat('https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/fraud/calculations/ridehailing_user_cancel_order_check/',CAST(uco.id AS varchar)) AS link,
uco.meta.country,
uco.meta.city_id,
uco.meta.order_id,
uco.meta.user_id,
CAST(json_extract_scalar(uco.input, '$.data.driver_id')AS bigint) AS driver_id,
uco.decision.decision,
row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY CAST(uco.meta.order_id AS varchar)||CAST(uco.meta.city_id AS varchar) ORDER BY uco.id DESC) AS rownumber
FROM archive_analytical.ridehailing_user_cancel_order_check uco
WHERE uco.created_hour >= CAST(DATE_ADD('month', -1, current_date) as date)
AND uco.meta.country = 'gb'
  )
 SELECT
      cot.driver_id,
      a.country_code,
     cot.created, 
     cot.order_id, 
     cot.state, 
     cot.price,
     cot.price /r.rate AS price_eur,
     CASE WHEN l."TYPE" = 'full' THEN cot.price 
     		WHEN l."TYPE" = 'partial' THEN l.amount 
     		ELSE 0 END 
     			AS amount_refunded,
     CASE WHEN l."TYPE" = 'full' THEN cot.price /r.rate WHEN l."TYPE" = 'partial' THEN l.amount/r.rate ELSE 0 END AS amount_refunded_eur,
     c.decision
      FROM ng_public.company_order_try cot 
      JOIN checks AS c ON cot.city_id = c.city_id AND cot.order_id = c.order_id AND cot.driver_id = c.driver_id AND rownumber = 1
      JOIN ng_public.admin_system_city a ON cot.city_id = a.id
      LEFT JOIN ng_public.currency_exchange_rates r ON cot.price_currency = r.currency AND date(r.valid_on) = cot.created_date - INTERVAL '1' DAY
      LEFT JOIN ng_public.invoicing_refund_refund_log l ON l.order_id = cot.order_id AND l.city_id = cot.city_id AND l.action_timestamp >= CAST(DATE_ADD('month', -1, current_date) as date)
      WHERE 
      cot.created_date 
--      = date('2025-02-01') 
      >= CAST(DATE_ADD('month', -1, current_date) as date)
      AND cot.state = 'client_cancelled'
      AND a.country_code = 'gb'
      --AND cot.driver_id = 1320723   
   ) AS x GROUP BY 1,2{noformat}

Hi, [~accountid:712020:a7a7d4bc-10ca-44a0-a22e-fa8752330abd] 

I've shared the file with you. 🙏 

Long story short, the driver had some disputes with the FO regarding payouts and missed targets. The situation escalated to a point where multiple versions of the story emerged, making it difficult for me to track - nor should I have to. 🙃 

In October, the driver used the car as a bargaining tool, refusing to return it to the FO to get what he believed was rightfully his. Despite our policy of not blocking drivers at the FO’s request, we ended up doing so in November when the FO asked us to. This led the driver to accuse us of being manipulative and dishonest. Acknowledging our mistake, we unblocked him, but he still didn’t return the car.

In our correspondence, the driver admitted to having the car but refused to return it, claiming that the FO (his employer) was not the actual owner. He attempted to drag us into this dispute. (FYI: he had “taken” another car the previous year under similar circumstances.)

The FO then filed a criminal complaint against him for stealing the car. The driver was unaware of this. Later, the FO forwarded us the state police’s decision to initiate criminal proceedings, and the car was officially declared missing in the databases. Based on this, we blocked him again.

The driver, upset by this, contacted us demanding an explanation. We informed him that the block was due to:

# The initiation of criminal proceedings against him.
# The car being officially reported as missing.
# His own admission that he had the car.

Things remained quiet for a while - until the driver noticed that the car was back on the road under an active license. What had happened? The police found the car abandoned in the woods and returned it to the FO.

The driver then started questioning the block, arguing that if the car was recovered, why was he still blocked? However, we had received no official confirmation that the criminal proceedings had been dropped. If we had given in, he would have insisted that we were once again influencing the settlement between him and the FO in the FO’s favour. The state police wouldn't notify us since we are a third party; only the FO or the driver himself could provide that information.

At this point, the driver started questioning whether a criminal case was ever filed and claimed it was fabricated. He also began demanding details about the case. When we reached out to the police to ask if we could disclose any information to the driver, they confirmed that we could not share such details with the driver. Similarly, when the driver asked the police directly, they gave him the same response.

Now, we find ourselves in a situation where the driver is demanding information that we shouldn't have access to in the first place - except that the FO had sent us the police’s decision. My gut feeling is that if we say the FO shared the information with us, he’ll blame them for disclosing it to third parties (driver doesn’t know where did we get the info from). So we should be strategic in our answer. 😉

Hi [~accountid:712020:714baa0e-ddd0-4776-8064-c5a5d3ae37aa] As promised, please see below my comments on the agreement: 

* *Parking* - The agreement contains the following clause relating to parking: ”_NOVA Acoustics Ltd will require a parking space for a small van type vehicle within a reasonable distance to the test area. Where site parking is unavailable any parking charges including fines shall be chargeable to the Client.” Are you ok with this?_
* *Timelines for Deliverables* - I would  like to raise your attention to the following clause: “_ALL acoustic consultancy services, noise surveys or technical reports will be provided to the client within 28 days of the environmental measurements being undertaken.”_ Is this what you’ve agreed?
* *Payment Terms* - The agreement contains the following clauses: “A_ll payments will be made by The Client within 30 days of the date of The Consultant’s invoice” “No report shall be submitted to the client by the company until full funds are cleared unless agreed in writing.”_ Is this what you’ve agreed? I would usually recommend agreeing payment on delivery of the report or 50% upfront and 50% after the delivery of report. Otherwise, if we’re not happy with the report, we would have no leverage. 
* *Cancellation Terms* - FYI, we would be liable to pay the following cancellation fees: 
** If the Consultancy and/or Testing Services is cancelled or postponed by the Client within one business day of the agreed test date then 100% of the quoted Fee is chargeable
** If the Consultancy and/or Testing Services is cancelled or postponed by the Client within three business days of the agreed test date then 50% of the quoted Fee is chargeable.
* *Suspension* - FYI, they are able to suspend the service where there are overdue payments, stoppage, delay or interruption of work during the period of The Project as a result of strikes, of the industrial location, other industrial disputes, breakdowns, accident, sickness, failure by The Client to give adequate instructions or approvals, or any cause whatsoever beyond the control of The Consultant. However, in that case we would still be liable to pay them. 
* *Liability -* their liability is capped at £1m, which is good. However, their liability would cease upon delivery of any reports. This means that they would have no liability for any product or process we implement on the basis on the findings of this project. Are you ok with this?
* *Indemnity -* We’re required to indemnify them for all loss or damage or expense suffered by any third party for which they may become liable in connection with the carrying out this project. I would suggest adding a caveat to this stating that we would not be liable for any damage or expense suffered by a third party arising from a breach of their terms of the agreement or their non-compliance with any laws or regulations. 
* *Sub-contracting* - They are entitled to sub-contract their work out wherever necessary. I would suggest checking if they plan to sub-contract this work? If so, we should ask them to be liable for all actions and omissions of their sub-contractors. 

Let me know if you would like to discuss any of the above points.

Technically, Braze does support SCIM, or at least it has endpoints for User management. 
Therefore, even if custom SCIM application can not be setup within Okta, we can move the automation to Workflows and create a “pseudo-scim” instead:

* User creation can be handled via [endpoint|https://www.braze.com/docs/api/endpoints/scim/post_create_user_account/#prerequisites]
** only hurdle is to map out all the appropriate fields such as: department, permissions, etc.
*** _this has to be done per workspace/dashboard_
** Once mapped out, we can then automate a Jira ticket that would be pushing for proper approvers automatically according to a subsystem (eg. see Databricks)
*** each workspace/dashboard has stakeholder approval + managers approval (or partners handler)
* Managing/removing accesses/permissions can be handled by editing the users data via [api call|https://www.braze.com/docs/api/endpoints/scim/put_update_existing_user_account]
** Have separate workspaces as *groups* on Okta (eg. rides, fleet, business)
*** _these can also be re-certified with a campaign_
**** if revoked, group is removed from the user which triggers automation to edit the users permissions and removing the single permission from them
***** visa versa if the user is provided new permissions
* User account lifecycle in general - deactivation etc.

*Why?*
Reduce the amount of manual work for two teams

* *IT* no longer handles these manually
* *Lifecycle* no longer has to manually manage user creation as well as permission granting
* Hygiene is handled by Okta - recertification if a user no longer needs access to a certain dashboard/permission, or upon deactivation, [a user is deactivated/deleted|https://www.braze.com/docs/api/endpoints/scim/delete_existing_dashboard_user]
* less tickets
* users do not see blank page but actual proper workspace/dashboard



*Potential issues*

* multiple subsystems and approvers
** if one approver denies the request the whole request is cancelled

* • although workflow can handle multiple subsystems at once

Hi! [~accountid:5d50390ec6b9320d9ea58352]we are moving out of having public global T&Cs. Taking Estonia as an example, the answer is: 

No, but it could be, because despite the [Drivers T&Cs |https://bolt.eu/en-ee/legal/tnc-drivers/?category=rides]do not explicitly mention public or banking holidays as a reason for delaying payouts, there is a clause (6.3) from where it could be interpreted as implied that transfers may depend on banking operations, which are normally affected by public holidays as it's a common financial industry practice that transactions might be postponed if they fall on such non-working days as typically banks do not operate on public or banking holidays. 

The clause I think might be interpreted to imply that such payouts are subject to normal banking operations, which typically do not occur on holidays is the following:

_6.3. Bolt transfers the amounts received to Bolt’s bank account as In-app Payments in the previous week to the Driver’s bank account generally by the fourth calendar day of the following week. If the Driver requests a review of In-app Payments, Bolt may transfer the received amounts after the review has been completed._

The use of _"generally by the fourth calendar day"_ is giving us some flexibility, suggesting that transfers are subject to conditions, which might include banking holidays.

Therefore, it's reasonable to deduce that payouts scheduled around these days might encounter delays due to the closure of banking institutions.

I am willing to assume all markets T&Cs will have something similar around this, but its a matter of confirming one by one depending on the need.

The user is reporting a double-charge because of incremental authorization.
Incremental authorization in card payments refers to the process of requesting an additional authorization on a customer’s card when the original authorized amount is insufficient to cover the final transaction cost. This typically happens in scenarios where the final amount of the transaction is not known upfront or may change.

I have checked the case and everything looks good on Bolt’s end. The pre-authorization has been released to the customer. 
You can ask the customer to reach out to their bank in order to confirm the authorized funds have been released. Their bank can locate the funds with the authorization date and amount.

[~accountid:712020:62d2d09a-02e2-437d-abbd-86f5be2b5737] Please find our analysis below:

*Suspended business activities* (under the presumption that the obligation to submit tax adjustments arises at the moment of resumption of business activities)

We suggest making payments upon resumption of activities. Messages informing about such possibility should be sent, but their content must be agreed with Baker, especially regarding names of the bonuses, justification for postponing the payment, etc. The wording must be cautious, as conditioning the bonus payment in this manner could imply that it is a tax compensation not a bonus. Also the obligation to inform Bolt about resumption must be imposed on the fleets/drivers as Bolt is unable to track it.

*Terminated business activities*

It is recommended to verify whether the fleet continues its activities under a different entity (by examining drivers' data, registered office, board members, owners etc.). If it does, payment should be made to the new entity. If not, it can be assumed that the cooperation has been terminated.

The reasoning of the above recommendation is following:
Under competition law, a company that holds a dominant position in the market is prohibited from engaging in discriminatory practices against its contractors. Such conduct may be classified as an abuse of dominant position, which is subject to significant penalties - the company may face a fine of up to 10% of its annual turnover. Additionally, individuals in managerial positions may be subject to a fine of up to PLN 2 million.

Fleets may argue that by continuing our collaboration with the new fleet operating under the setup of the previous fleet, we have implicitly consented to the assignment. 

However, according to our assessment the public interest criterion is lacking in discussed situation and circumstances of the compensations are unusual and not aimed at discrimination, thus it is rather unlikely that the Office of Competition and Consumer Protection (UOKiK) will take action. Furthermore, you have already made a business decision not to pay compensation to entities that no longer cooperate with Bolt and therefore, the decision to pay or not to closed entities does not significantly increase the already existing risk.
More probable than UOKiK’s actions is that individual contractors may seek compensation to which they might be potentially entitled on the grounds of discrimination. However, as mentioned above, such risk already exists due to the solution you agreed upon with Baker regarding Bolt’s previous contractors, consequently only the scope of allegedly entitled entities would be expanded.

*Please keep in mind that legal team may only provide you with recommendations and the decision regarding course of action remains at the discretion of business.*

h3. Cause: Continuous Inserts from Running DM Task

{{sync_diff_inspector}} uses the primary key (PK) to divide the dataset into chunks and compare checksum values.
If there are continuous inserts from the source MySQL to TiDB, there will be a slight delay between MySQL and TiDB,
which makes the last checksum count different.

As you can see, two different queries were run to check the status of the counts.
The first query shows that {{2193295786}} (MySQL) is greater than {{2193295773}} (TiDB),
but a moment later, the total counts are the same: {{191200814}}.

I have checked all four large tables and found this behavior only in two tables: {{task}} and {{billing_trail}}.

h3. Does stopping replication on the source MySQL or stopping the DM task solve the problem? Yes and No.

Stopping data synchronization on replication or the DM task will resolve the count difference issue; however, it will introduce a new problem.
We have a *4-hour SLA* to sync data to *Kafka* and *Presto*. Checking the {{task}} table (117G) alone takes *40 minutes*, and we have the following large tables:

h3. *Tables*

{noformat}+---------------------------+----------------------------------+--------------------+-----------+
| TABLE_SCHEMA              | TABLE_NAME                       | TABLE_COLLATION    | size in G |
+---------------------------+----------------------------------+--------------------+-----------+
| taxify_delivery_invoicing | billing_trail                    | utf8mb4_general_ci | 134G      |
| taxify_delivery_invoicing | organic_event                    | utf8mb4_general_ci | 252G      |
| taxify_delivery_invoicing | record                           | utf8mb4_general_ci | 780G      |
| taxify_delivery_invoicing | task                             | utf8mb4_general_ci | 117G      |
+---------------------------+----------------------------------+--------------------+-----------+
{noformat}

The inspection won't finish within 4 hours.
However, manual checks confirm that there is no difference in {{min}}, {{max}}, or {{count}} for the {{organic_event}} and {{record}} tables,
so I believe the data is consistent.

Some analysis on the {{session timed out}} issue in the RA:

When entering the username and enrolment code, the user gets this error:

!image-20250212-114108.png|width=600,height=160,alt="image-20250212-114108.png"!

This is because the RA approaches session management differently than the CA:

{quote}*The default timeout works the same way. However, there's a session keep-alive service which lowers the session timeout and actively re-validates the session to keep the RA user logged in while being able to detect when the browser is closed and terminate the session.*{quote}

When submitting the enrollment form, this request in the background fails:

!image-20250212-114509.png|width=83.33333333333334%,alt="image-20250212-114509.png"!

Unfortunately nothing about this is printed to the server log. However chrome dev tools actually helps us out with debugging here:

!Screenshot 2025-02-12 at 13.49.44.png|width=100%,alt="Screenshot 2025-02-12 at 13.49.44.png"!

That’s the reason. Even though we had configured the RA to operate over http for now, the cookie is still specified with the {{secure}} attribute. This won’t be an issue with the production instance, because we will be using HTTPS for connecting to the RA. The issue exists only for the test environment.

“Services” as per the clause above means the B4B services in this case, which for Bolt Rides PL are localised in this entity. CAST(json_extract_scalar(d.input, '$.data.order.order_id')AS bigint) AS order_id,
row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY CAST(json_extract_scalar(d.input, '$.data.order.order_id') AS varchar)||CAST(json_extract_scalar(d.input, '$.data.order.city_id') AS varchar) ORDER BY d.id DESC) AS rownumber
FROM glue.archive_analytical.driver_overcharge_check d
CROSS JOIN UNNEST (d.decision.actions) AS a(actions)
WHERE d.created_hour >= DATE_ADD('month', -3, CURRENT_DATE)
AND a.actions = 'set_price_to_zero'
)
SELECT 
date_trunc('month',co.created_date) AS month_order,
CASE WHEN o.actions IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS overcharge_to_zero_check,
approx_distinct(co.order_id,0.0041) AS count_orders,
round(sum(pot.value/co.eur_currency_rate),0) AS sum_tips_eur
FROM ng_public.etl_denormalized_commerce_orders AS co
LEFT JOIN overcharges AS o ON co.order_id = o.order_id AND co.city_id = o.city_id AND co.user_id = o.user_id AND o.created >= CAST(DATE_ADD('month', -3, current_date) AS date) AND o.rownumber = 1
LEFT JOIN ng_public.pricing_order_tips pot ON pot.city_id = co.city_id AND pot.order_id = co.order_id AND pot.created_date >= CAST(DATE_ADD('month', -3, current_date) AS date)
WHERE co.created >= CAST(DATE_ADD('month', -3, current_date) AS date)
AND co.created_date >= CAST(DATE_ADD('month', -3, current_date) AS date)
AND pot.value = co.partner_price
AND pot.value > 0
AND o.actions IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY 1,2{noformat}

Hi [~accountid:712020:b25a56d4-6d1e-4c68-83ca-ebdda2617c3e] 

You have opened the pandoras box with your relatively simple question - how do the rentals payments work? 

There are multiple teams involved. 
The rentals vertical - creates orders, suborders and assigns order pricing. 
Customer payments team - Creates payments and and governs the bolt balances. 
Fraud team - Chooses to keep or not to keep the pre-auth. Chooses when or if to end the ride in case of multiple failed payments. 

What makes the rentals payments different from other verticals is the “suborder”. Suborders are created daily and when the payment exceeds a threshold. (in Estonia the threshold is 50€). For every suborder there is a new payment. 
We also have to keep in mind the rentals vertical often deals with partners like Traficar in Poland and Miles in Germany. These partners might have slightly different payment rules, however the general payment processing logic should remain the same. 



* Mentioned example: [https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/rentals-carsharing/orders/edit/global/17829632?tab=details|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/rentals-carsharing/orders/edit/global/17829632?tab=details]
Price: 208,48 PLN
Uncovered amount: 99,48 PLN

That’s an excellent question. Will investigate the case with payment engineers and let you know as soon as possible. 

* I also saw an example of an order in which the rent was due for a few days. We didn't capture any payment from the user, but we still let him start the rent (like this one: [https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/rentals-carsharing/orders/edit/global/17497672?tab=details|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/rentals-carsharing/orders/edit/global/17497672?tab=details]).

The user used the rental for 38 days and the payments were failing causing the Bolt Balance debt. It’s an old order and it’s no longer possible. The Fraud team has processes in place to avoid it from happening with collaboration with local ops teams. If the user has a certain number for failed payments then the ride is finished (safely). 

* Or from more recent history, this order([https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/rentals-carsharing/orders/edit/global/23233768?tab=details|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/rentals-carsharing/orders/edit/global/23233768?tab=details]), where we didn't try to charge the full amount.

This is one of the simpler cases. We tried to charge the full amount but the customers payment failed for 553.31 PLN due to insufficient funds. The user is not able to rent another car again until the bolt balance debt has been eliminated. 

Please let me know if you have any more questions and please allow me to loop back to you regarding some of these topics. 

Cheers,

*General note*: please bear in mind that for the time being only taxi category is live. Bolt is not determining the price but we are simply reflecting the prices as set forth under the taxi regulations. Price finally paid the passenger reflects the one displayed on the taximeter. 

Price adjustment clause in GR have been localised and tailored to mitigate the risk of qualifying as a transportation service provider in GR and practices to flag fraud cases should be consistent with  wording enshrined in the T&Cs. 



# *PRICE ADJUSTMENT* 

*Issue:*  avoid any reference to price determination/price adjustment as this would increase the risk to be considered as a transportation service provider.



*Solution:* We recommend that you avoid any reference to price determination/price adjustment as this would increase the risk to be considered as a transportation service provider.
